passage: During Class 6 morning break, I watched Deepak wave at Mahima as she crossed the corridor. She kept walking, head down, holding her books. Deepak's hand fell. He sat down heavily on the bench and said to me, “She didn't even look.” I didn't know what to say. Later, I saw Mahima at the water stand with her eyes red, maybe because of a headache or worry about the test. I don't know. When she came back, Deepak said, “Hi,” and she smiled and answered. Deepak grinned and looked embarrassed at once. “I guess she just didn't see me,” he told me.

qa.q: Who waved at Mahima in the corridor?
qa.a: Deepak.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Mahima did not respond to his wave, and what did he later conclude?
qa.a: He felt hurt and snubbed, but after she smiled and replied later, he thought she might simply not have seen him.

qa.q: What could Deepak do next time someone ignores his hello?
qa.a: He could check again later, as he did, before deciding it means unfriendliness.

qa.q: How might Mahima have been feeling when she passed the corridor?
qa.a: She may have been worried or unwell, since her eyes were red later, so she was probably busy with her own thoughts.

grounding: A missed hello may be inattention rather than snub, and checking twice before feeling hurt is wise.

passage:
Monday. Avni gave a big smile to the new boy Jomon at the gate, but he looked past her. Avni went quiet all morning, thinking he didn't like her.

Wednesday. She said hello again in the corridor. Jomon jumped, took out earphones and said, “Oh, sorry, I was listening to a story!” Avni laughed, a bit surprised.

Friday. Jomon waved to her from far away at the canteen, and Avni waved back. “I thought you ignored me,” she told him. “I did not see you on Monday,” he said. “I'm still learning where everyone is.”

qa.q: What was Jomon doing on Wednesday when Avni said hello again?
qa.a: He was listening to a story with earphones.

qa.q: What did Avni first think when Jomon looked past her at the gate?
qa.a: She thought he did not like her and felt hurt, so she stayed quiet all morning.

qa.q: What did Avni do that helped her read the situation better?
qa.a: She said hello again on Wednesday instead of deciding on Monday that he was cold.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt as a new boy on the first days?
qa.a: He was probably busy learning where everyone is, so he missed the smile without meaning to be unfriendly. 🙂

grounding: A missed hello may be inattention, and a child checks twice before feeling hurt.

passage: Seema, you're sulking because your friend walked past without saying hi. Let your Joseph Appachan tell you something. When I was eleven, in Kottayam, my best friend Mathew walked straight past me at the Sunday market. No wave, no smile, nothing. I was furious. I didn't speak to him for three days. On the fourth day I finally marched up and said, “Why did you ignore me?” He blinked. “When? I broke my glasses that week. I couldn't see anyone further than my own hand.” Three days of sulking, for nothing. So now I always look twice, and ask once, before I decide someone meant it.

qa.q: Why couldn't Mathew see young Joseph at the market?
qa.a: Mathew had broken his glasses that week.

qa.q: What was young Joseph feeling after Mathew walked past?
qa.a: He felt hurt and furious, believing his best friend had deliberately ignored him.

qa.q: What choice did Joseph finally make, and what did it show?
qa.a: He asked Mathew directly why he'd ignored him, which showed the missed hello was about broken glasses, not a snub.

qa.q: How might Mathew have felt during those three days?
qa.a: Mathew may have felt confused or hurt that his friend wasn't speaking to him, without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a child reading a missed greeting as a snub when it was inattention, and checking before feeling hurt.

passage: The corridor between periods was a crush of bags and elbows, and the bell had already gone. Nilesh spotted Gopika coming the other way, balancing a huge cardboard model of a heart, and called, “Hi, Gopika!” She walked straight past, eyes fixed on the model. Nilesh's smile dropped. Great. She's still annoyed about the cricket. He almost didn't look back. Then he did. She was edging sideways through the crowd, lips moving as if counting steps, one arm hooked round the model to keep it from being crushed. At lunch he asked, “Did you hear me this morning?” She stared. “You said hi? I didn't hear a thing. I was just trying not to drop the aorta.”

qa.q: What was Gopika carrying?
qa.a: Gopika was carrying a huge cardboard model of a heart.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when Gopika walked past?
qa.a: Nilesh felt hurt and snubbed, thinking she was still annoyed about the cricket.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that stopped him feeling hurt for nothing?
qa.a: He looked twice, noticed how hard she was concentrating on the model, and asked her at lunch.

qa.q: What was that moment in the corridor like for Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika was focused on not dropping the model in the crowd and never heard Nilesh's hello.

grounding: Shows a child reading an unanswered hello as a snub in a busy corridor, and checking twice before feeling hurt.

passage: Every morning in the lift of their Chandigarh apartment block, Baljeet said a big “Good morning!” to Francis Uncle from the seventh floor. Every morning, Francis Uncle only nodded, once, without a word. Baljeet began to think the old man didn't like children. Maybe I'm too loud. One Sunday, Baljeet watched from the balcony as Francis Uncle walked round the garden. He nodded at the guard, the gardener, the vegetable seller, even the dogs. The same short nod, the same small smile at the corner of his mouth. That evening, in the lift, Baljeet nodded first. Francis Uncle's eyes crinkled, and for the first time he said, “Good evening, young man.”

qa.q: Which floor does Francis Uncle live on?
qa.a: Francis Uncle lives on the seventh floor.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when Francis Uncle only nodded each morning?
qa.a: Baljeet felt unsure and a bit hurt, wondering if the old man didn't like children or found him too loud.

qa.q: How did Baljeet check his first reading?
qa.a: He watched Francis Uncle greet everyone with the same nod and small smile, and saw it was simply his friendly way.

qa.q: What might Francis Uncle have felt when Baljeet nodded first?
qa.a: Francis Uncle probably felt pleased and understood, since he answered with crinkled eyes and warm words.

grounding: Shows a child reading a neighbour's silent nod as coolness, and watching more to find it was his friendly way of acknowledging others.

passage:
"Ayesha, why did you ignore me yesterday?"
"Ignore you? When?"
"By the library. I waved with both hands. You walked straight past."
"Yesterday… Oh no. I'd just got my maths paper back. I wasn't seeing anything."
"You looked right at me."
"I looked at the wall, probably. I was doing sums in my head, trying to find where I lost eight marks."
"So… not a snub?"
"Rukmini, you're my first-bench partner. Why would I snub you?"
"I thought maybe you were cross because I sat with Mona at lunch."
"I didn't even notice that. Next time, wave in front of my face."
"I'll wave twice. Then check."

qa.q: Where did Rukmini wave at Ayesha?
qa.a: By the library.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling after the missed wave?
qa.a: Hurt and worried, fearing Ayesha was cross about lunch with Mona.

qa.q: What habit could help Rukmini the next time a hello is missed?
qa.a: Check twice, by waving again or asking, before deciding it was a snub 🙂

qa.q: What was going on for Ayesha during that walk past the library?
qa.a: Ayesha was anxious about the maths paper and busy doing sums in the head, so the wave went unseen.

grounding: It shows a child reading a missed hello as a snub, and asking to find it was inattention, not coolness.
